body.text: Before leaving for Asia last week, U.S. President Donald Trump suggested that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, raising speculation that the two leaders would see each other again after seven years. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reinforced the expectation when he said that Trump was “serious” about meeting Kim.
In the end, the widely anticipated meeting did not materialize during Trump’s whirlwind Asia trip. He nevertheless indicated that it could take place “at some point.”
Why was there no Kim-Trump meeting in China? Will it be held anytime soon?

The relationship between Trump and Kim has been a rollercoaster ride. Initially, the two were openly hostile, trading aggressive insults throughout 2017, the first year of Trump’s first term. Trump mocked Kim as “Little Rocket Man,” while Kim ridiculed Trump as a “mentally deranged dotard.”
Their relationship took a dramatic turn when they started to exchange letters in 2018. “He wrote me beautiful letters. And they’re great letters. We fell in love,” Trump said at the time.
During his first term, Trump met Kim three times: in Singapore in 2018, in Hanoi in 2019, and at the Korean Demilitarized Zone later that same year.

Weeks before Trump’s latest Asia trip, there appeared to be diplomatic efforts to arrange another Kim-Trump summit. Washington seemed to be softening its stance toward Pyongyang. For example, Rubio argued that North Korea’s nuclear ambitions should be viewed differently because Kim is primarily concerned with regime survival rather than territorial expansion.
Washington also withheld its support for a U.N. resolution condemning North Korea’s human rights abuses for the first time in 21 years.
Despite these conciliatory gestures, a fourth Kim-Trump meeting did not happen. Several factors may help explain why.

First and foremost, Trump does not have much to offer. Kim’s position is secure at home, while North Korea has cultivated increasingly close relations with both Russia and China. Kim has sent more than 10,000 North Korean soldiers to fight alongside Russian forces in the war with Ukraine. And he recently visited the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened border bridge.

These developments have strengthened Kim’s strategic position. U.S. policy emphasizes denuclearizing North Korea, but Pyongyang wants to be recognized as a nuclear state and officially end the Korean War. Kim has little incentive to meet Trump merely for a photo opportunity without securing meaningful concessions.
It takes two to tango. If a more confident Kim is not enthusiastic about another summit, it is unlikely to happen anytime soon.

Second, there may simply have been insufficient time to organize such a high-profile meeting in China. A summit like this requires extensive advance preparation, including security arrangements, diplomatic coordination, and agreement on at least some basic understandings.

Chinese and American diplomats were preoccupied with preparations for Trump’s historic meeting with Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China. Arranging another historic encounter between Trump and Kim would have required additional and complicated multilateral coordination.

There is also a broader geopolitical consideration. A Kim-Trump meeting on Chinese soil could have enhanced Beijing’s international standing. At the same time, it could have allowed Trump to claim a major diplomatic achievement in China. Beijing might have welcomed the former while remaining cautious about the latter.

Third, concerns in South Korea may have complicated Washington’s deliberation. South Korean officials watched the diplomatic maneuvering in China with apprehension. They were concerned that Trump might negotiate regional security arrangements with Xi and Putin without consulting U.S. allies.

Seoul is particularly sensitive to developments on the Korean Peninsula that take place without its participation. Days before the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun asked his Chinese counterpart to help bring North Korea back to the negotiating table. He stressed that no summit should make decisions concerning the Korean Peninsula without Seoul’s participation.

For Seoul, the prospect of a Kim-Trump meeting is not necessarily unwelcome. However, South Korea does not want to be sidelined in discussions that could fundamentally affect its interests. U.S. efforts to engage Pyongyang must therefore take South Korean concerns into account.

Considering all these factors, there is little reason to be optimistic about another Kim-Trump summit in the near future. The two leaders may still meet again, and Trump clearly seems interested in keeping that possibility alive. But the strategic calculations have changed considerably since their first encounters. Kim is in a stronger geopolitical position, North Korea’s nuclear capabilities have expanded, and the regional security environment has become more complicated.

Ultimately, the question is not when Trump will meet Kim, but whether Kim sees enough benefits in meeting Trump – and whether Washington is prepared to make the concessions necessary to bring him to the negotiating table.
